extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, European patent attorneys, EPO examiners, and practitioners working with the EPC
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Articles 52, 53 and 54 of the European Patent Convention, setting out the substantive patentability requirements (novelty, inventive step, industrial application), subject-matter exclusions and the EPC definition of novelty (state of the art). Useful for evaluating whether a claimed invention meets EPC standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: New (Novelty) as a patentability requirement (Article 52)
rubrics_metrics.description: European patents shall be granted for inventions provided that they are new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty is a core substantive requirement under Article 52; the EPC's Article 54 supplies the legal definition of 'new' and the applicable prior art (state of the art).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step as a patentability requirement (Article 52)
rubrics_metrics.description: European patents shall be granted for inventions provided that they involve an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventive step is a separate substantive requirement from novelty and is assessed independently; note that some prior disclosure categories (e.g., Article 54(3) earlier-filed EP applications) are relevant to novelty but not to inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Susceptible of industrial application (Industrial applicability) (Article 52)
rubrics_metrics.description: European patents shall be granted for inventions provided that they are susceptible of industrial application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires that the invention can be made or used in some kind of industry; it is one of the three fundamental EPC patentability requirements alongside novelty and inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoveries, scientific theories and mathematical methods excluded (Article 52(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Discoveries, scientific theories and mathematical methods are not regarded as inventions and are excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are treated as non‑inventions under Article 52(2); whether a claim that includes such subject-matter can be patentable depends on whether it has technical character beyond the excluded matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic creations excluded (Article 52(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic creations are not regarded as inventions and are excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purely aesthetic subject-matter lacks the technical character required for patentability; if an aesthetic feature contributes technical effect it may be considered differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schemes, rules and methods for performing mental acts, playing games or doing business excluded (Article 52(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Schemes, rules and methods for performing mental acts, playing games or doing business are not regarded as inventions and are excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business methods and mental acts as such are excluded; patentability may be possible where such schemes are implemented with a technical character or technical means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programs for computers excluded (Article 52(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs for computers are not regarded as inventions and are excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exclusion applies only to computer programs 'as such'; computer-implemented inventions that provide a technical solution or have technical character may be patentable (see Article 52(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentations of information excluded (Article 52(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentations of information are not regarded as inventions and are excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure presentations of information lack technical character; if a presentation contributes to a technical effect it may fall outside the exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: "As such" limitation on Article 52(2) exclusions (Article 52(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusions in Article 52(2) apply only to the extent to which a European patent application or European patent relates to such subject-matter or activities 'as such'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'as such' limitation means that subject-matter excluded in principle (e.g., computer programs) can be patentable when combined with technical character — for example, computer programs combined with technical character (computer-implemented inventions) may be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morality and public order exclusion (Article 53(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions immoral or contrary to public order ('ordre public') are excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 53(a) excludes inventions that offend morality or public order; assessment depends on whether the claimed subject-matter contravenes these principles under EPC case law and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant or animal varieties and essentially biological processes excluded (Article 53(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Plant or animal varieties and essentially biological processes for their production are excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 53(b) bars plant/animal varieties and essentially biological processes; however, microbiological processes and the products thereof are not excluded (explicit exception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for treatment of the human or animal body by surgery or therapy excluded (Article 53(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods for treatment of the human or animal body by surgery or therapy and diagnostic methods practised on the human or animal body are excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important exception: this exclusion does NOT apply to products, particularly substances or compositions, for use in such methods. This permits purpose-limited product claims for medical uses (e.g., 'Swiss-type' claims or EPC 2000 second medical use claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: State of the art definition for novelty (Article 54(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of the art comprises everything made available to the public by written or oral description, use or in any other way before the date of filing of the European patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any disclosure made publicly prior to the filing date (written, oral, by use, or otherwise) can negate novelty. The precise timing (before filing date) is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earlier-filed, later-published European patent applications for novelty only (Article 54(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of European patent applications filed before the date referred to in Article 54(2) but published on or after that date is part of the state of the art for novelty purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 54(3) prior art is applicable only to novelty assessment and not to inventive step; it prevents double-patenting but cannot be used to attack inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: First and further medical use / purpose-limited product claims (Articles 54(4) and (5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow purpose-limited product claims for known substances or compositions when used for new medical applications (first and further medical use claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles 54(4) and (5) enable claiming new therapeutic uses of known compounds via purpose-limited product claims (e.g., Swiss-type or EPC 2000 second medical use formulations), preserving novelty for new medical indications.
